title: Modi's Red Bandhani Safa Continues a Decade-Long Independence Day Turban Tradition
excerpt: For India's 80th Independence Day, the Prime Minister chose a maroon tie-and-dye turban rooted in Rajasthani and Gujarati textile traditions, marking his 13th consecutive Red Fort address.
body:
• PM Modi wore a bright red tie-and-dye safa with yellow and white Bandhani patterns for India's 80th Independence Day at the Red Fort
  • The turban was paired with a white kurta-pyjama, a chocolate-brown sleeveless vest, and pocket squares in the colors of the national flag
  • This marked Modi's 13th consecutive Independence Day address from the Red Fort — making him the second Prime Minister to reach that milestone
  • The Bandhani technique, a centuries-old tie-and-dye craft from Rajasthan and Gujarat, has become a recurring feature in Modi's ceremonial headgear choices

A Red Safa for the 80th Independence Day

Prime Minister Narendra Modi arrived at the Red Fort on Saturday wearing a bright red tie-and-dye turban dotted with yellow and white Bandhani patterns — his latest statement in a tradition that has made his Independence Day headgear a subject of national attention for over a decade.

The safa, with its long trailing end in the style of traditional Rajasthani headwear, was paired with a classic white kurta-pyjama, a chocolate-brown sleeveless vest, and pocket squares in saffron, white, and green — the colors of the Indian national flag. The ensemble was completed with black formal shoes.

The Bandhani Craft Behind the Turban

Bandhani, also known as bandhej, is a centuries-old tie-and-dye technique practiced primarily in the states of Rajasthan and Gujarat. The process involves plucking the fabric with fingernails into thousands of tiny bindings, which when dyed and released create distinctive dotted patterns. The technique dates back centuries and remains a living craft tradition, with artisans in cities like Jamnagar, Bhuj, and Jodhpur continuing to practice the painstaking process by hand.

The craft has been a recurring feature in Modi's ceremonial headgear. His very first Independence Day turban as Prime Minister in 2014 was a bright red Jodhpuri bandhej, and the technique has appeared in various color combinations throughout his tenure. The consistency is seen as a deliberate nod to the textile heritage of his home state of Gujarat and neighboring Rajasthan.

13 Years at the Red Fort

Saturday's ceremony marked Modi's 13th consecutive Independence Day address from the Red Fort ramparts, making him only the second Prime Minister after Jawaharlal Nehru to reach that milestone. The speech centered on themes including India's economic transformation from the "Fragile Five" to the fastest-growing major economy, free online coaching for middle-class families, and the 150th anniversary of the national song Vande Mataram.

In a moment that drew attention beyond the speech, Modi broke protocol to walk toward a group of children near the Red Fort audience, picking up a cap that had fallen from a child's head in what was described as a spontaneous gesture.

A Visual Vocabulary of Regional Craft

Over the years, Modi's Independence Day turbans have drawn from regional textile traditions across India, creating what observers describe as a visual vocabulary of cultural diversity. The choices have ranged from saffron motifs to multicolored Rajasthani leheriya patterns, tricolor-inspired designs, and various bandhani styles.

Last year, for the 79th Independence Day, he wore a vibrant saffron turban. For Republic Day 2026, he opted for a richly colored Rajputana-style safa in deep crimson and maroon with golden motifs.

The practice has become part of the visual identity of India's Independence Day celebrations, with each year's choice generating discussion about regional craftsmanship and the stories woven into India's textile heritage. For the Indian diaspora watching celebrations from abroad, the turban offers a tangible connection to the cultural traditions that remain central to India's national identity.
